guide.title: Parioli, Rome: Villa Ada, the Auditorium and the 1960 Olympic quarter
guide.intro: Parioli is the second quartiere of Rome, numbered Q. II, and it lies outside the Aurelian Walls in Municipio Roma II. It is not one of the twenty-two rioni of the historic centre: it is a residential quartiere laid out mostly in the twentieth century, and an address matters here more than a neighbourhood name. Inside its boundaries stand the Auditorium Parco della Musica with two museums in it; Villa Ada Savoia, a hundred and sixty hectares of former royal park with a fort, the remains of a town of Latium vetus, a wartime bunker and two catacombs under it; Villa Glori, made into a memorial park in 1924; the village and two Nervi venues built for the 1960 Olympics; the Grande Moschea di Roma; three twentieth-century parish churches; and three bridges, one of them Ponte Milvio.

sections.heading: What is in Parioli, and what is not
sections.body:
Parioli's edges are rivers and named streets, and it.wikipedia's article on the quartiere gives them exactly. To the north it meets Q. XVIII Tor di Quinto across the Tiber, from Ponte Milvio to the mouth of the Aniene, and Z. I Val Melaina across the Aniene, from that confluence to Ponte Salario. To the east it meets Q. XVII Trieste across via Salaria, from Ponte Salario to viale Liegi. To the south it meets Q. III Pinciano along the whole of viale Liegi, the whole of viale dei Parioli and the whole of viale Maresciallo Pilsudski as far as via Flaminia. To the west it meets Q. I Flaminio along via Flaminia, from viale Maresciallo Pilsudski to piazzale Cardinal Consalvi at Ponte Milvio.

That matters because several things a visitor would file under Parioli sit on the far side of one of those lines. The catacombs of Priscilla, the complex of Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura and the mausoleum of Santa Costanza are all across via Salaria, in Q. XVII Trieste; Villa Torlonia is in Q. V Nomentano; Villa Balestra and the recording studios and theatre at piazza Euclide are Pinciano's; the Roman villa excavated during the Auditorium's building works is in Flaminio, although it stands on the same site and adjoins the complex. Via Flaminia itself is a boundary for the whole length of Flaminio's eastern edge. Its history still belongs to this corner of Rome: the consular road was laid out in 220 to 219 BC by Gaius Flaminius Nepos and ran from Porta Flaminia to Ariminum, and Porta Flaminia is the gate known today as Porta del Popolo, which stands in the rione Campo Marzio.

Two names are traps. The Stadio Flaminio is in Parioli despite its name: it.wikipedia states in terms that the stadium belongs administratively to the quartiere Parioli, at whose western end it stands, viale Tiziano running alongside the administrative boundary with Flaminio. And the Villaggio Olimpico is a zona urbanistica inside Parioli rather than a unit of its own.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station for this quartiere. The Roma to Civita Castellana and Viterbo railway runs through it, and it.wikipedia's article on the quartiere names Campi Sportivi, Acqua Acetosa and Monte Antenne among its stops. Steer by addresses rather than by the quartiere name, because the quartiere is large.

The fixed points are these. The Auditorium Parco della Musica, with the MUSA instrument museum and the Museo Aristaios inside it, is at Viale Pietro de Coubertin 10, 00196 Roma, the address the operator prints in its own footer. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives Villa Ada Savoia's entrances as via Salaria 267, 273 and 275, via di Ponte Salario, via di Monte Antenne and via Panama, and gives Villa Glori's as piazzale del Parco della Rimembranza and viale Maresciallo Pilsudski. The Grande Moschea di Roma is on viale della Moschea. The Teatro Parioli-Costanzo is at Via Giosue Borsi 20. San Roberto Bellarmino is on piazza Ungheria and San Luigi Gonzaga at Via di Villa Emiliani 15, 00197 Roma. San Valentino and the Villaggio Olimpico are both on viale XVII Olimpiade, the village's main axis. The Stadio Flaminio is on viale Tiziano and the Palazzetto dello Sport on largo Apollodoro, off it.

Each of the three bridges stands in more than one unit. Ponte Milvio carries the old via Flaminia over the Tiber at piazzale Cardinal Consalvi. Ponte Flaminio carries Corso di Francia over the Tiber between Parioli and Q. XVIII Tor di Quinto. Ponte Salario carries via Salaria over the Aniene, in the quartieri Parioli and Trieste and the zona Val Melaina. Corso di Francia, viale dei Parioli, viale Tiziano and piazza Ungheria are useful for finding your way.

sections.heading: Opening hours and tickets
sections.body:
Four things in Parioli publish hours, and they are worth planning around; most of the rest do not.

The Auditorium Parco della Musica gives its own opening as October to March, 11:00 to 20:00, and 11:00 to 20:00 on Sundays and holidays; April to October, 11:00 to 20:00, and 10:00 to 20:00 on Sundays and holidays. On days with a show in the Cavea the Auditorium closes at 16:00. The Museo Aristaios inside it is free, and its own page gives every Saturday 11:00 to 18:00, or 11:00 to 20:00 in summer time, and every Sunday and public holiday 10:00 to 18:00, or 10:00 to 20:00 in summer time, adding that during particular events the exhibition spaces may be closed. San Luigi Gonzaga's parish gives mass on weekdays at 07:30 and 19:00, on Saturday at 09:00 and 19:00, and on Sundays and holidays at 09:00, 10:30, 12:00 and 19:00.

For MUSA, for Villa Ada Savoia, for Villa Glori and for San Roberto Bellarmino, no source states opening hours, so none are given here. The Fonte di Anna Perenna is in the care of the Soprintendenza Speciale and is visited on guided tours by booking. The bunker under Villa Ada has been open to visitors since April 2016 under an agreement between the Comune and the Associazione Roma Sotterranea, which runs the visits. No source states its hours or prices. For the catacombs of the Giordani, of Sant'Ilaria and of Trasone, no source states whether they can be visited, so none is given here.

Three places in Parioli are shut to visitors and the reason is on the record in each case. The Palazzina Reale in Villa Ada has been the seat of the embassy of the Arab Republic of Egypt since 1997 and is a working diplomatic mission; you see it from the park. Forte Antenne is abandoned and its own record gives it as not visitable. The Ipogeo di Villa Glori is likewise given as not visitable.

faq.question: Is the Auditorium Parco della Musica in Parioli, and what is its address?
faq.answer: Yes. The operator's own footer gives Viale Pietro de Coubertin 10, 00196 Roma. Renzo Piano designed the complex, which was built between 1995 and 2002 on a site of 55,000 square metres. The operator gives the Sala Santa Cecilia 2,744 seats, the Sala Sinopoli 1,133, the Sala Petrassi 673 and the Teatro Studio Borgna 300, with the open-air Cavea taking 3,000 to 5,000 and the Giardini pensili Claudio Abbado covering 38,000 square metres. It was named for Ennio Morricone by a resolution of Rome's city council in 2020.

faq.question: Why is the Stadio Flaminio in Parioli and not in Flaminio?
faq.answer: Because of where it stands rather than what it is called. it.wikipedia says in terms that despite the name the stadium belongs administratively to the quartiere Parioli, at whose western end it stands, viale Tiziano being adjacent to the administrative boundary with the quartiere Flaminio. Antonio Nervi designed it with structural engineering by his father Pier Luigi Nervi, and it was inaugurated on 19 March 1959 in a live television broadcast, on the site of the Stadio Nazionale, for the 1960 Olympic football tournament.

faq.question: Can you go into Villa Ada, and is the royal palace open?
faq.answer: The park is open and the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives its entrances as via Salaria 267, 273 and 275, via di Ponte Salario, via di Monte Antenne and via Panama. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. The Palazzina Reale is a different matter: built in 1873 to 1875 and a royal residence from 1904 to 1946, it was acquired by the Arab Republic of Egypt in 1997 and has been the seat of its embassy since. It is a working diplomatic mission and is not open to visitors, who see it from the park.

faq.question: What is inside Villa Ada besides the park?
faq.answer: Monte Antenne, the hill in the north of the park, carries the remains of Antemnae, a fortified town of Latium vetus that Romulus is said to have stormed after the raid that followed the rape of the Sabine women, and Forte Antenne, one of the fifteen forts built round Rome between 1877 and 1891. The Bunker di Villa Ada Savoia was cut into the tufa of the hill called delle Cavalle Madri between 1940 and 1942 as an air-raid shelter for the royal family. Two catacombs, the Giordani and Sant'Ilaria, run under the park, and a light-well of a third, the Catacomba di Trasone, opens in the courtyard of the Palazzina Reale.

faq.question: Is anything in Parioli free to enter?
faq.answer: The Museo Aristaios inside the Auditorium states free entry on its own page, with hours on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. The parks cost nothing: Villa Ada Savoia at a hundred and sixty hectares, Villa Glori at twenty-five, and the four thousand two hundred square metres of the public garden at Villa Grazioli, reached from via Bruxelles and viale di Villa Grazioli. So does the Fontana dell'Acqua Acetosa, a papal fountain reached by a stair below street level, and so do the three bridges.

faq.question: Where should I eat in Parioli?
faq.answer: Parioli is residential and has restaurants, cafes, bars, hotels and shops along viale dei Parioli and around piazza Ungheria. No source names a particular one.

places.name: Auditorium Parco della Musica Ennio Morricone
places.address: Viale Pietro de Coubertin 10, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: A concert complex of three lead-clad halls arranged around an open-air cavea, with a walkable terrace running round the whole. The operator gives the Sala Santa Cecilia 2,744 seats, the Sala Sinopoli 1,133, the Sala Petrassi 673 and the Teatro Studio Borgna 300; the Cavea takes 3,000 to 5,000 and the Giardini pensili Claudio Abbado cover 38,000 square metres. Its published hours are October to March, 11:00 to 20:00, and 11:00 to 20:00 on Sundays and holidays; April to October, 11:00 to 20:00, and 10:00 to 20:00 on Sundays and holidays. On days with a show in the Cavea the Auditorium closes at 16:00.
places.history: Renzo Piano designed it and it was built between 1995 and 2002 on a site of 55,000 square metres. It opened on 21 April 2002 with the Sala Sinopoli, and the rest of the complex and the Sala Santa Cecilia followed on 21 December 2002 with the orchestra of the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia under Chung Myung-whun. Rome's city council named it for Ennio Morricone by a resolution in 2020. The Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia has held its concert season here since 2003, the Fondazione Musica per Roma manages the site, and the Festa del Cinema di Roma has been held here since 2006. The complex also holds the AuditoriumGarage exhibition space of 655 square metres, the 200 square metre AuditoriumArte, and a permanent sound installation, the Sound Corner. A Roman villa came to light during the building works in 1995 and its remains stand on the same site, adjoining the complex.

places.name: MUSA - Museo degli strumenti musicali dell'Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia
places.address: Viale Pietro de Coubertin 10, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: The Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia's collection of musical instruments, inside the Auditorium. About 130 instruments are shown together with some fifty luthier's accessories, in a workshop that visitors can see into and where the luthiers who look after the collection work. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The present gallery opened in February 2008. Among the named holdings are the Stradivari violin known as the Toscano, made in 1690 and one of five instruments of the so-called quintetto Mediceo made for Grand Prince Ferdinando de' Medici; a viola by David Tecchler, a German-born luthier working in Rome in the first half of the eighteenth century; and a mandolin from the private collection of Queen Margherita di Savoia, who left it to the Accademia.

places.name: Museo Aristaios (Collezione Sinopoli)
places.address: Viale Pietro de Coubertin 10, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: A collection of Greek and Italic antiquities in the Sala del Peduncolo of the Auditorium, over 300 square metres, with a fit-out by Alvisi Kirimoto. Entry is free. The museum's own page gives every Saturday 11:00 to 18:00 in standard time and 11:00 to 20:00 in summer time, and every Sunday and public holiday 10:00 to 18:00 in standard time and 10:00 to 20:00 in summer time, adding that during particular events the exhibition spaces may be closed to the public.
places.history: The museum opened in December 2012 and holds the 161 works bought by the Ministry from the heirs of the conductor and collector Giuseppe Sinopoli, under a valorisation agreement between the Ministry, Roma Capitale and the Fondazione Musica per Roma. The ceramics run from Minoan and Mycenaean through Geometric, Corinthian, Laconian and East Greek to Attic black-figure and red-figure, Italiote red-figure and indigenous Daunian ware, with a Cycladic marble vase, Etruscan and Magna Graecia bronze vessels and votive statuettes. Attic pieces include work by Lydos, the Lysippides Painter, the circle of Nikosthenes, the Syleus Painter and the Eretria Painter.

places.name: Villa Ada Savoia
places.summary: A hundred and sixty hectares of former royal park, managed by Roma Capitale. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places it in Municipio II, quartiere Parioli, and gives the entrances as via Salaria 267, 273 and 275, via di Ponte Salario, via di Monte Antenne and via Panama. About eighty per cent of it is wooded and the rest grass and shrub; the dominant tree is the umbrella pine, with holm oak, laurel, olive, elm, maple, poplar and many oaks, and a metasequoia imported in 1940. Red squirrels, moles, hedgehogs, wild rabbits and crested porcupines live in it, and a parrot colony near the former royal villa. A ring path of about four kilometres with interpretive panels runs round the public area. Since 1994 the lake has hosted the summer world-music series Roma incontra il mondo. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: On 25 July 1943, after the Grandi motion, the king summoned Mussolini to Villa Ada, where he was arrested and driven away in an ambulance. The estate was partly unified by Prince Luigi Pallavicini at the end of the 1780s, who had it laid out by the French architect Auguste Chevalle de Saint-Hubert with Francesco Bettini; on the Presidenza del Censo plan of 1839 much of the former Pallavicini estate appears as Potenziani property, and in 1872 it was sold to Vittorio Emanuele II, who enlarged it by buying neighbouring vineyards. In 1878 the villa was sold to a count of Swiss origin whose name the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives as Tellfner; it.wikipedia gives the name as Giuseppe Telfener and says the estate took the name Ada from his wife. Vittorio Emanuele III repurchased it in 1904 and it was a royal residence until 1946; the part toward via Salaria was acquired by the state demanio in 1957. The Sovrintendenza names the Casale detto La Finanziera, now the seat of WWF; the Fienile, used as a riding centre; the Casale delle Cavalle Madri, named for its Savoy-era use as a shelter for brood mares from the Quirinale stables; Villa Polissena; the Scuderie reali; the Villa Reale; the Casino Pallavicini; the Tempio di Flora; and le Tribune along the boundary wall on via Salaria. The Tempio di Flora is an eighteenth-century coffee-house by the Casino Pallavicini, its neoclassical pronaos and facade concealing an apsed rear that repeats the colonnade and looks down on a small amphitheatre-shaped hollow with a late nineteenth-century cast iron fountain at its centre.

places.name: Palazzina Reale di Villa Ada
places.summary: The neoclassical royal house in the middle of Villa Ada. It has been the seat of the embassy of the Arab Republic of Egypt since 1997, so it is a working diplomatic mission and is not open to visitors; you see it from the park.
places.history: It was built between 1873 and 1875 by Gennaro Petagna with the engineer Guglielmo Castelnuovo, and was the residence of Vittorio Emanuele III and his family from 1904 to 1946. The Arab Republic of Egypt acquired it in 1997.

places.name: Bunker di Villa Ada Savoia
places.summary: An air-raid shelter cut into the tufa of the hill called delle Cavalle Madri in Villa Ada, about 350 metres in a straight line from the Palazzina Reale. It has been restored and open to visitors since April 2016 under an agreement between the Comune di Roma and the Associazione Roma Sotterranea, which runs the visits. No hours and no prices are given here.
places.history: It was built between 1940 and 1942 as a shelter for the royal family. There is no underground link to the Palazzina, which is why it was given a drive-in entrance where cars could be parked inside; it has armoured doors, air filtration, water and stores, and a second exit up a spiral stair from a small circular structure nearby that also ventilates it. No plans or cost schedules for its construction survive. It was abandoned after the war and heavily graffitied before the restoration.

places.name: Forte Antenne
places.summary: A fort of two and a half hectares on Monte Antenne, in the north sector of Villa Ada, near the confluence of the Aniene and the Tiber. Its own article places it in the quartiere Q. II Parioli, in the territory of the Municipio Roma II. It is abandoned, Roma Capitale owns it, and it is given as not visitable.
places.history: It is one of the fifteen forts built round Rome between 1877 and 1891, in what the source calls Prussian style. Its own article dates the fort 1880 to 1884 in the infobox and 1882 to 1891 in the text. Its strategic role ended in 1919; it was used as a store by the Reggimento Radiotelegrafisti into the 1940s and then decommissioned. The demanio ceded it to the Comune in 1958 for the 1960 Olympics, to be used as a campsite, but private dwellings had already gone up inside the fort and the campsite was built in the surrounding park instead.

places.name: Antemnae
places.summary: The remains of a fortified town of Latium vetus on Monte Antenne, the hill now partly occupied by Forte Antenne inside the park of Villa Ada, above the confluence of the Aniene and the Tiber and looking down on via Salaria near Ponte Salario. It is in the care of the Sovrintendenza capitolina. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina glosses the name ante amnem, before the river.
places.history: Its people were the Antemnati, and Plutarch, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, Virgil and Silius Italicus all mention the town. Rome under Romulus stormed and took it after the Antemnates raided Roman territory following the rape of the Sabine women. Antonio Nibby identified the site in 1834; it was excavated in 1878, in 1978 and in 1986.

places.name: Catacomba dei Giordani
places.summary: A catacomb on the left side of via Salaria, under Villa Ada, in the quartiere Parioli, in the care of the Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra. No source states whether it can be visited, so none is given here.
places.history: It is datable between the second half of the third century and the first half of the fifth, on inscriptions carrying the extreme dates 269 and 436, and is named for the Giordani, the family that owned the ground. Marcantonio Boldetti and Giovanni Marangoni brought it to light in 1720 and took it for the catacomb of Trasone; the identification was settled by the 1966 excavations of the Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra, above all by the finding of the tomb of the martyr Alexander, whom several historical sources place in coemeterio Iordanorum.

places.name: Catacomba di Sant'Ilaria
places.summary: A small catacomb on the left side of via Salaria, under Villa Ada, in the quartiere Parioli. A narrow gallery joins it to the neighbouring cemetery of the Giordani. No source states whether it can be visited, so none is given here.
places.history: The connecting gallery to the Giordani was opened around the eighteenth century by corpisantari, relic-hunters. Antonio Bosio visited the catacomb at the end of the sixteenth century and described some of its paintings in his posthumous Roma sotterranea. Little of the decoration survives: of the scene in the so-called arcosolio dell'auriga there remain only the heads of the horses and a running figure.

places.name: Catacomba di Trasone
places.summary: A catacomb on via Salaria at the junction with via Yser, in the quartiere Parioli, entered through a manhole. It grew out of a sandstone quarry turned over to burial and has galleries on five levels. It runs almost entirely beneath Villa Grazioli and its park, and a light-well of it is visible in the courtyard of Villa Ada's Palazzina Reale. No source states whether it can be visited, so none is given here.
places.history: It is named for Trasone, a wealthy Roman of the time of Diocletian who converted to Christianity and is named in the passio of St Susanna. Ancient sources also call it Coemeterium Thrasonis ad s. Saturninum, for the martyr Saturninus buried there, whose above-ground basilica was still visible at the end of the sixteenth century.

places.name: Villa Glori (Parco della Rimembranza)
places.address: Piazzale del Parco della Rimembranza, Roma RM
places.summary: Twenty-five hectares of park on the hill of the same name, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina places in Municipio Roma II, quartiere Parioli. The entrances are piazzale del Parco della Rimembranza and viale Maresciallo Pilsudski. A fortified casale survives from the period when the hill was vineyard and hunting ground rather than a suburban villa. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Some seventy volunteers crossed into papal territory on 20 October 1867 and entrenched themselves in a vineyard on Monte Cacciarello, where the papal zouaves overran them during the night of 22 to 23 October. Enrico Cairoli died there and his brother Giovanni, gravely wounded, died soon after. The vineyard belonged to Vincenzo Glori, whose name the hill kept, and Cesare Pascarella made the episode into twenty-five Romanesco sonnets published in 1886. The master plan of 1883 first proposed a large green space here and expropriation began; the monument to the fallen of 1867, an antique Pietrasanta marble column on a rustic travertine base, was inaugurated in 1895; the Comune repossessed part of the park in 1905; and by a resolution of 23 October 1923 the area was made a Parco della Rimembranza for the dead of the First World War. Raffaele de Vico designed it in eight months and the park opened on 18 May 1924. At piazzale del Mandorlo stand the monument to the Cairoli brothers, the brick structure that held a dry branch of the almond tree under which Enrico Cairoli died, and a cippus to servicemen who died in peacetime; viale dei Settanta is named for the men of the 1867 fight, and a plaque to the carabinieri killed at Nassiriya stands behind Paolo Canevari's Uomo Erba. Three wooden pavilions built in 1929 for a summer colony survive. Between 1997 and 2000 the Comune installed works by contemporary artists: Dompe, Mattiacci, Mochetti, Caruso, Castagna, Kounellis, Nunzio and Staccioli in 1997, Uncini and Canevari in 2000.

places.name: Ipogeo di Villa Glori
places.summary: A Roman hypogeum near Villa Glori, in the care of the Sovrintendenza capitolina and given as not visitable.
places.history: It was found by chance in 1794. Several of its rooms were used as tombs, some of them chamber tombs divided into niches, and it carries frescoes of Hercules, Bacchus and the Dioscuri.

places.name: Fontana dell'Acqua Acetosa
places.summary: A papal fountain in the flat called the Acqua Acetosa, in the quartiere Parioli, where the Tiber makes a deep bend. It sits below street level and is reached by a stair. The front is an exedra with three niches, each carrying the Chigi arms of six mounts beneath an eight-pointed star above a small basin fed by a spout, with a tympanum and a plaque above. The name comes from the ferruginous spring here, which sixteenth-century Romans knew as acqua acetosa.
places.history: In 1613 Paul V had the water analysed; it was found potable and held good for complaints of the kidneys, stomach, spleen and liver, and some bottled it to sell in the city. In 1619 he had Giovanni Vasanzio build a fountain, recorded by the plaque still low on the wall, though at that date the source was simply a wall the water ran from. Innocent X had it restored and Alexander VII commissioned the present fountain; the attribution to Bernini is probably false, and Andrea Sacchi and the architect Marco Antonio De' Rossi have both been proposed. In 1712 Clement XI ordered a further restoration after complaints of reduced flow, long queues and worsening water, recorded on a plaque above the central niche; the commission included the papal physician Giovanni Maria Lancisi and the architect Egidio Maria Bordoni. Paul V's dedicatory epigraph reads Renibus et stomacho, spleni corique medetur / Mille malis prodest ista salubris aqua: this healthful water is medicine for the kidneys, the stomach, the spleen and the heart, and is good for a thousand ills.

places.name: Fonte di Anna Perenna
places.address: Via Guidubaldo del Monte, Roma RM
places.summary: A votive fountain of the fourth century BC dedicated to the goddess Anna Perenna, rectangular, built in tufa blocks and brick, with an altar, found at a depth of between 6.2 and 10.3 metres below street level. It is in the care of the Soprintendenza Speciale and is visited on guided tours by booking.
places.history: It was discovered in 1999 during works for a car park in the quartiere Parioli, at via Guidubaldo del Monte, which runs off piazza Euclide, and it had remained in use until the sixth century AD. The find fixed the site of the sacred grove of Anna Perenna that Ovid names in the Fasti, and produced an exceptional quantity of evidence for magical practice over many centuries. The material from the adjoining cistern is displayed at the Terme di Diocleziano, in the rione Castro Pretorio.

places.name: Villaggio Olimpico
places.summary: The housing quarter built for the athletes of the 1960 Olympics, on the flat between the hill of Villa Glori and the Tiber. Its main axis is viale XVII Olimpiade and the Corso di Francia viaduct cuts it north to south. It is a zona urbanistica inside the quartiere rather than a unit of its own.
places.history: It stands on the site of a wartime shanty settlement of evacuees called campo Parioli, which the 1960 Games were the occasion to clear. It was built in 1958 and 1959 to designs by Vittorio Cafiero, Adalberto Libera, Amedeo Luccichenti, Vincenzo Monaco and Luigi Moretti, funded by the state employees' pension fund, the Comune di Roma and CONI; the completed buildings were handed to INCIS and allotted by competition to state employees. It was inaugurated in 1960 for the XVII Olympiad.

places.name: Stadio Flaminio
places.summary: A stadium on viale Tiziano, built for the football tournament of the 1960 Olympics. Despite the name it belongs administratively to the quartiere Parioli, at whose western end it stands, viale Tiziano being adjacent to the boundary with the quartiere Flaminio. The pitch is 105 by 70 metres and the total area 21,600 square metres; the stadium was built for 42,000 places. No source states whether it can currently be visited.
places.history: Antonio Nervi designed it with structural engineering by his father Pier Luigi Nervi, and it was inaugurated on 19 March 1959 in a live television broadcast, on the site of the Stadio Nazionale, at a cost of about 900 million lire of the day. From the 1970s it was used by the Italy national rugby team and by Rugby Roma Olimpic, and at times by Lazio, Roma, Lodigiani and Atletico Roma. The FIGC has conducted the ground since 26 February 2014 and redevelopment proposals have been under discussion.

places.name: Palazzetto dello Sport (PalaTiziano)
places.summary: An indoor arena on largo Apollodoro, off viale Tiziano, built for the 1960 Olympics. Its own article places it in the quartiere Parioli. The building surface is 2,650 square metres and the total 4,800. No source states whether it can be visited outside events, so none is given here.
places.history: Annibale Vitellozzi conceived and designed it in 1956 with structural engineering by Pier Luigi Nervi, and it was built in 1956 and 1957 for events of the XVII Olympiad by the contractor Ingg. Nervi e Bartoli Spa. Pallacanestro Virtus Roma used it on and off until 2018. It was refurbished in 2022 and 2023 at a cost of 3,200,000 euro.

places.name: Chiesa di San Valentino al Villaggio Olimpico
places.summary: The parish church of the Villaggio Olimpico, on viale XVII Olimpiade, in the quartiere Parioli. It is built in exposed brick with a steel and glass roof and is preceded by a statue of an angel that reproduces one of the statues of Ponte Sant'Angelo.
places.history: The parish was constituted on 2 May 1962 by the decree Ludis olimpicis solemniter. Before the present building went up the parish was visited by Paul VI on 5 June 1969. The church was built between 1983 and 1986 to a design by Francesco Berarducci and consecrated by Cardinal Ugo Poletti on 23 November 1986; John Paul II visited on 16 February 1992.

places.name: Chiesa di San Roberto Bellarmino
places.summary: A rationalist parish church on piazza Ungheria. Its article, citing the Diocese of Rome, places it in the quartiere Parioli, within the boundaries of the Municipio Roma II. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Clemente Busiri Vici built it between 1931 and 1933 and it was opened for worship on 10 June 1933 and consecrated in May 1959. It is dedicated to Robert Bellarmine, canonised in 1930. Pius XI erected the parish on 13 May 1933 with the apostolic constitution Quae maiori religionis and entrusted it to the Jesuits, who were replaced by diocesan clergy in 2003; it has been a cardinalatial title since 1969. John Paul II visited on 2 March 1980.

places.name: Chiesa di San Luigi Gonzaga
places.address: Via di Villa Emiliani 15, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A parish church in the quartiere Parioli, run by the Comboni missionaries. The parish gives mass on weekdays at 07:30 and 19:00, on Saturday at 09:00 and 19:00, and on Sundays and holidays at 09:00, 10:30, 12:00 and 19:00.
places.history: The foundation stone was laid on Thursday 18 July 1929 at a ceremony led by Cardinal Basilio Pompilj, and the architect Enrico Castelli built the church in 1929 as the church of the adjoining Carmelite convent. The whole complex was sold to the Comboni missionaries in 1958. The church became a parish on 7 January 1963 by the decree Percrescente incolarum numero, its territory taken from the parishes of San Roberto Bellarmino and Sacro Cuore Immacolato di Maria, and the interior was restored at that time. John Paul II visited on 6 November 1988, and a relic of the heart of St Aloysius Gonzaga was enthroned on 13 March 2012. A side chapel holds a fresco of St Thomas painted by Kiko Arguello in 1993.

places.name: Grande Moschea di Roma
places.summary: The mosque of Rome and the seat of the Centro islamico culturale d'Italia, on viale della Moschea at the foot of the Monti Parioli and Monte Antenne, next to the Acqua Acetosa sports facilities. It occupies 30,000 square metres of ground and holds up to 12,000 worshippers, and about 30,000 to 40,000 on major feasts such as the Feast of the Sacrifice. Its style is described as postmodern and Islamic.
places.history: It was designed by Paolo Portoghesi, Vittorio Gigliotti, Sami Mousawi and Nino Tozzo. Building began in 1984 and the mosque opened on 21 June 1995.

places.name: Teatro Parioli-Costanzo
places.summary: A working theatre on via Giosue Borsi, and since 2024 also a theatre school for children and young people directed by Raoul Bova and Rocio Munoz Morales.
places.history: The building went up in 1938 as a cinema and opened as a theatre on 29 December 1958, the first piece being Schnitzler's Girotondo staged by the Ernesto Calindri and Vivi Gioi company. It was renamed Teatro Parioli-Costanzo on 20 February 2024.

places.name: Villa Grazioli
places.summary: A public garden of 4,200 square metres in the Municipio II, in the quartiere Parioli, reached from via Bruxelles and viale di Villa Grazioli. It is what survives of the original park after the subdivision of the 1920s. The former Badoglio villa on the same ground is a working embassy and is not part of the garden a visitor enters.
places.history: The area is documented as Villa Lecci on the plan of 1839 and on the 1845 to 1846 plan of the cantoni of Rome drawn for Baron von Moltke, and passed to the Grazioli Lante della Rovere family at the end of the nineteenth century. In 1937 Clemente Busiri Vici was commissioned to build a villa here for General Pietro Badoglio, and on the night of 7 to 8 September 1943 Badoglio met the American general Maxwell Taylor there, the day before the armistice of Cassibile was announced. According to roma2pass.it the former Badoglio villa now houses the embassy of the People's Republic of China. The Catacomba di Trasone runs almost entirely beneath this villa and its park.

places.name: Ponte Milvio
places.summary: The bridge that carries the old via Flaminia over the Tiber at piazzale Cardinal Consalvi, at Parioli's western corner. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes six arches on five piers with triangular cutwaters, a core of Grotta Oscura tuff faced in pietra sperone and travertine, and gives it as accessible to the public. Vehicle traffic was cut from 1951 and stopped altogether in 1978.
places.history: Livy mentions the bridge in 207 BC, when it was still timber; the censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus rebuilt it in masonry in 110 to 109 BC. Volturcius was arrested on it during the Catilinarian conspiracy, and the battle of 312 was fought at it. Garibaldians blew the northern central arch in 1849 and Pius IX had it restored; Valadier had rebuilt the two outer arches in 1805, and Callixtus III added the square tower that carries the Borgia plaque. The habit of attaching padlocks to the bridge spread from the central lamp-post after the film Ho voglia di te; a lamp-post broke under the weight in July 2007; the Comune installed posts and chains for the purpose; and the locks were removed for good in September 2012.

places.name: Ponte Flaminio
places.summary: An arch bridge carrying Corso di Francia over the Tiber, 254.94 metres long and 27 metres wide. It stands in the quartieri Parioli and Q. XVIII Tor di Quinto.
places.history: Armando Brasini designed it with the engineer Aristide Giannelli. It was begun in 1938 and finished in 1951, planned as a northern entrance to the capital and intended to be called Ponte XXVIII Ottobre. From 1960 it has connected to the Corso di Francia viaduct.

places.name: Ponte Salario
places.summary: The bridge that carries via Salaria over the Aniene, the last bridge the Aniene passes under before it joins the Tiber. It stands in the quartieri Parioli and Trieste and in the zona Val Melaina. It was rebuilt in 1930.
places.history: Ancient writers name the bridge repeatedly. Livy, in Ab Urbe condita VII.9, places the Gauls camped three miles from Rome on the via Salaria beyond the bridge over the Aniene; Hannibal camped on the plain before it in 211 BC; Ricimer halted there in 472 and Witiges in 537; and it was badly damaged in 544.

entries.name: Auditorium Parco della Musica Ennio Morricone
entries.note: Renzo Piano's three lead-clad halls round an open-air cavea, built 1995 to 2002 and named for Ennio Morricone by a council resolution in 2020.

entries.name: Museo Aristaios (Collezione Sinopoli)
entries.note: The 161 Greek and Italic works from Giuseppe Sinopoli's collection, opened in December 2012 in the Auditorium's Sala del Peduncolo, with free entry at weekends.

entries.name: MUSA - Museo degli strumenti musicali dell'Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia
entries.note: About 130 instruments, among them the Stradivari of 1690 known as the Toscano, shown beside a working luthiers' workshop that visitors can see into.

entries.name: Villa Ada Savoia
entries.note: A hundred and sixty hectares of former royal park with a four-kilometre ring path and panels; the king had Mussolini arrested here on 25 July 1943.

entries.name: Bunker di Villa Ada Savoia
entries.note: The royal family's air-raid shelter of 1940 to 1942, cut into the tufa with a drive-in entrance, open to visitors since April 2016 through the Associazione Roma Sotterranea.

entries.name: Antemnae
entries.note: The remains of a town of Latium vetus on Monte Antenne, identified by Antonio Nibby in 1834 and dug in 1878, 1978 and 1986.

entries.name: Forte Antenne
entries.note: One of the fifteen forts built round Rome between 1877 and 1891, two and a half hectares on Monte Antenne, abandoned and given as not visitable.

entries.name: Villa Glori (Parco della Rimembranza)
entries.note: Twenty-five hectares laid out by Raffaele de Vico and opened on 18 May 1924, on the hill where the papal zouaves overran the Cairoli volunteers in October 1867.

entries.name: Fontana dell'Acqua Acetosa
entries.note: A ferruginous spring that Paul V had analysed in 1613; the exedra with three niches and the Chigi arms was commissioned by Alexander VII.

entries.name: Fonte di Anna Perenna
entries.note: A votive fountain of the fourth century BC found in 1999 under a car park, which fixed the site of the sacred grove Ovid names in the Fasti; visits are by booking.

entries.name: Stadio Flaminio
entries.note: Antonio and Pier Luigi Nervi's stadium for the 1960 Olympic football tournament, inaugurated on 19 March 1959 and built for 42,000 places.

entries.name: Villaggio Olimpico
entries.note: Housing built in 1958 and 1959 by Cafiero, Libera, Luccichenti, Monaco and Moretti for the XVII Olympiad, on the site of the wartime campo Parioli.

entries.name: Ponte Milvio
entries.note: Timber in Livy's account of 207 BC and rebuilt in masonry by the censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus in 110 to 109 BC; closed to vehicles since 1978.

entries.name: Grande Moschea di Roma
entries.note: Designed by Portoghesi, Gigliotti, Mousawi and Tozzo, begun in 1984 and opened on 21 June 1995; no visiting hours are published.

The southern neighbour, across viale Liegi, viale dei Parioli and viale Maresciallo Pilsudski; it holds Villa Borghese and the Galleria Borghese.
The rione at the city end of via Flaminia, holding Porta del Popolo, the gate the Romans called Porta Flaminia, and Piazza del Popolo.
